Control Resonant, Arc Raiders, and more upgraded

Sony has announced it is expanding support for its QSSR graphics enhancer on base PS5 to six more PS5 games in the coming weeks.

Through a free update, the feature is live right now in Marvel's Spider-Man 2. In addition, the following titles will receive support for QSSR soon:

More games will receive QSSR support in the future too, as Sony continues to work with developers in implementing the visual enhancement technology. "Developers are just getting started," Sony states. with the PS5 Pro has had PSSR since launch, which was recently upgraded via new version, the QSSR tech is designed for the base PS5 system.

Ghost of Yotei and Marvel's Wolverine also support the feature.

News Sony Confirms Refined Version of Acclaimed PSSR Upscaler for Base PS5, with 'Remarkable' Potential

QSSR support in Marvel's Spider-Man 2 is live now, and head of technology at Insomniac Games, Mike Fitzgerald, told the PlayStation Blog you should spot improved image stability and sharpness across both the Fidelity and Performance modes in the game.

Remedy expects to have QSSR support added to Control Resonant in December, at which point the PS5 title will have a "more stable and detailed image". Here's a comparison video:

Embark Studios is supporting QSSR across both its multiplayer games, The Finals and Arc Raiders. Once the PS5 patch is applied, expect "increased sharpness, better environmental clarity and overall visual improvements". Here is another comparison video for Arc Raiders specifically:

When No Man's Sky is updated with QSSR support, it'll "render the universe in sharper, cleaner and more beautiful detail, while delivering the best possible framerate". The patch should become available in the next few weeks.

#4051. Frostpunk 2's The Surge DLC keeps the wintery apocalypse and adds in faction-clash-inducing electricity and sets a seasonally appropriate December release date

For the time being, the world of Frostpunk remains a hypothetical, even if it's one that seems just that little bit more likely than I'd like it to be given who's in charge of the world. But at the very least, there are pockets of hope to be found in Frostpunk 2, namely with its newly revealed next bit of DLC, The Surge, a name that has been bequeathed to it for incredibly obvious reasons. Oh, you need me to explain them? Fiiiiine.

You and your probably not so merry band of survivors have been trekking across the UK, when you end up at a "mysterious valley." Apparently some rumours have been going round about a "marvel left behind by history’s greatest mind - a relic with the potential to reshape the world itself." So you go off to look for it, and it essentially seems like this relic lets you use a whole bunch of electricity. Only, despite how useful this is for automating a bunch of work, various factions disagree over how it should be used, "while the secrets hidden within the valley prove far more difficult to uncover than anyone expected."

In terms of what you should expect from this DLC, for starters there's a new scenario to check out "set in an entirely new region, far beyond the borders explored in Frostpunk 2 so far." This relic is also implied to have come from the mind of one Nikola Tesla, you know, the electricity guy. There'll apparently be ways to utilise the Great Storm that's ruined the planet to "turn catastrophic whiteouts into valuable, harvested and stored resources." And you'll have some hidden treasures to find and mysterious to uncover in various nearby caves and ruins.

All sounds neat enough! And it's not too far away either. The Surge is currently slated for a seasonally appropriate December 14th release date. Let's hope no real world environmental disasters get in the way of that, 'ey? While you wait for it, you can wishlist the DLC on Steam.

#4050. Play as water and rain on wildfires in Atuel, a short, free game about the power and vulnerability of nature

Well, have you played Atuel? If not, you can do so within the next hour - it's a tiny, free, 25-minute walking sim, albeit one with little actual walking on account of you playing most of it as a river. More of a running sim, really.

Have You Played? is an endless stream of game retrospectives.

Technically, Atuel calls itself a "documentary game", and not without justification. While its sweeping Patagonian landscapes are rendered with a dreamy otherworldliness, and certain moments are downright mystic, the whole watery journey is based directly on the Atuel River that runs through western Argentina. As you drift downhill, taking control of water, clouds, and the local wildlife, you'll hear real-life scientists and historians monologuing on the Atuel and its relationship with the human cultures it's nourished. Mercifully, these are delivered with thoughtfulness as well as earnestness, maintaining the game's contemplative atmosphere without making it sound like the audio guide to a museum of Birmingham canals.

A few bends in, Atuel also takes on the climate crisis, directing you away from the soothing freshwater and into wildfires and parched riverbeds. I'd say this was preaching to the choir, at least for anyone who a) desires a functioning planet and b) learned about the water cycle in primary school, but then it isn't really preaching. Rather, developers Matajuegos weave between the beauty of the Earth and the need to protect it quite gracefully, and end their river tour on a more hopeful note than its darker moments may have intimated.

There's plenty else to leave an outsized impression in your memory matter: the understated, naturally-textured soundtrack, for instance, or the patiently gradual zoom-outs that slowly unveil the Andes' wild splendour. For me, and without wanting to undermine the importance or the accuracy of Atuel's environmental point, it was mainly just nice – therapeutic, even – to float through its gorgeous, surreal scenery like a cloud. And sometimes, as one. You can download it for free from Steam and Itch, with a pay-what-you-want option on the latter.

#4049. Silica, an FPS and RTS hybrid that mixes a smidge of Dune and Helldivers together, has left early access and entered 1.0

The concept of fusing an RTS and an FPS always sounds like a fun one, and since 2023 Martin Melichárek has been trying to make a new take on the combination under the watchful eye of DayZ devs Bohemia Interactive through Silica. Today marks the day that Silica leaves early access and enters 1.0, fully fleshing out its hybrid and mish mash of Dune's Arrakis and Helldivers' Terminids.

Digging into Silica a touch more deeply, it is a sci-fi shooter set on a planet where there's a fancy resource you're trying to mine that definitely isn't the spice. There are two warring factions competing for said resource, when, uh oh! Some bug-ish, giant aliens aren't very happy you're doing all that. So, you can either join the fray on the ground with some classic first-person shooting alongside your friends, or you can take the role of commander and dictate your artillery from above.

The 1.0 update obviously comes with a few additions, namely the Centauri Campaign, a "story-driven single-player experience set in the war for Baltarus. It opens with a cinematic intro and features fully voiced mission briefings and in-game dialogue. Between missions, a 3D planetary globe tracks the war as territory changes hands." Commanding your army should be a better experience now too, with the ability to "arrange units into formations, issue more precise movement and attack orders, and quickly select all units of the same type. Improved AI targeting and vehicle movement also help your armies operate more effectively in large-scale battles."

Beyond that, 1v1 matchmaking has been added in, where you can fight against another commander. The Steam Workshop sandbox tools have been expanded for building your own scenarios and sharing them with others. And there are a whole bunch of bug fixes, quality-of-life improvements and additions, and more. You can read about some of those in more detail in this handy little blog post. If you like what Silica is putting down, then you can pick it up on Steam.

"We’re introducing one of the top requested features"

It's time for achievements in original Xbox games! Microsoft is officially rolling them out for four games today, with more to come over time. They're referring to this as "one of the top requested features" from fans in recent memory.

The four games that are getting Xbox achievements today are as follows:

You'll be able to access achievements for these games when playing them on Xbox One, Xbox Series X and Xbox Series S - and the same applies for PC as well, as they're all now part of the PC backwards compatibility programme.

News 21 Original Xbox Games Are Coming To PC Via Backwards Compatibility Today (November 12)

There's one key thing you'll need to do to see these achievements though - update your Xbox console by going to Settings, System and then Updates. If you see a new update ready to download in there, you'll need to grab it.

Microsoft says that more original Xbox games will be getting achievements in the future, and that they've worked with the developers and publishers of these initial four titles to craft their achievement lists. If you've already made progress in any of the aforementioned games, you may find that some achievements pop automatically.

We'll leave you with a few more details on what Xbox is saying about them:

"The addition of achievements also apply when you play these games on XBOX One and XBOX Series consoles. Make sure to take the latest system update so you can start earning them. In some cases, achievements may unlock based on progress you’ve already made. We worked closely with each game’s developers and publishers as we designed the achievements to make sure they fit the spirit of each title. We plan to bring achievements to more original XBOX games over time."

"The games you’ve played are part of your history with XBOX. Bringing more of them to PC and adding achievements are a few ways we’re ensuring you can continue to play the games you love, wherever you may choose."

#4047. Zelda: A Link Between Worlds Listed As 'Playable With NSO', But Let's Not Jump To Conclusions

Nintendo's official website for the Zelda series has updated its entry for A Link Between Worlds with a mysterious 'Playable with Nintendo Switch Online' icon, leading some to believe that it's a hint of an upcoming expansion to the paid service. However, we're not so sure.

The site is home to a series timeline, listing every mainline game from the NES original through to the Ocarina of Time remake. The likes of A Link to the Past, Link's Awakening and Oracle of Seasons are all marked with a 'Playable on NSO' button and, indeed, you can play all of them on the service. A Link Between Worlds has been locked to the 3DS since its launch back in 2013, however. Not only is it decidedly not playable on Nintendo Switch Online, but there isn't even a library for the console.

However, there are just as many replies that seem to take a similarly cautious approach to us. You see, the button is missing on Oracle of Ages — a game that notably is on the NSO library — and none of the series' other DS games have any sign that they're playable, too. Hmm.

We're chalking this one up to a simple mistake, then — we wouldn't be surprised to see the message removed soon enough. There have been rumblings of a dual-screen addition to the NSO library ever since we first learnt about the Switch 2's bonus USB-C port (remember those mock-ups for an extra screen add-on?), but it feels very unlikely we'd find out like this.

Ah well, back to our 3DS copies we go, then...

#4046. GTA 6's In-Game Animated TV Series, Macca & Friends, Hints at the Game's Absurd Scope

I think this might be the one thing about GTA 6 that's really made me aware of the sheer scale of what Rockstar Games is cooking up.

Exclusively revealed via DiscussingFilm, an in-game, animated TV series named Macca & Friends has been revealed with the below teaser trailer:

What strikes me about this is that the show looks exactly like the sort of thing you would see on Adult Swim. It has similar vibes to other cartoons aimed at adults, like Aqua Teen Hunger Force or Rick & Morty.

What I mean is, this doesn't look like your typical throwaway gag that plays on a loop in the background. It looks like a full production on its own.

It's described as a "series" in the official blurb, so it seems this will have multiple episodes you can watch within GTA 6. The show "follows the adventures of Macca the Gator and his wetland friends across the state of Leonida."

This won't be the only thing you can tune into, either; according to Kinda Funny, there are multiple shows that have been created, including a "novela" and another animated show called The Johnsons.

They say Rockstar "hired an animation studio" to create these things, and that seemingly includes Macca & Friends.

If this is the sort of scope we can expect from just watching TV in GTA 6, it gets me excited about the level of detail and scope in the rest of the game.

#4045. The Citadel Project is a Thief-inspired dark fantasy, survival-horror lite stealth-em-up with some lovely shadows set in a medieval megastructure

You know, given the whole stealthy element of Thief-like immersive sims, I'm surprised there haven't been more of them with horror elements. There's Gloomwood, sure, but it's not as common as I'd like. That in turn then makes me curious about The Citadel Project, an immersive sim with some survival-horror elements set in a nasty, parasite-infected dark fantasy world, all apparently made by just one person.

In The Citadel Project, "the last line of defense built by the Ancient Kings in an attempt to preserve what remains of humanity in the face of the Great Storm." Some kind of evil force is ruining it from the inside, and you have to make your way through a medieval megastructure to figure out what happened. You aren't anyone special, "just a simple prisoner who manages to escape from a cell deep within the Citadel." Truthfully, the story sounds fine enough, I'm more smitten with the vibes put on display.

The shadows are what sells me, for the most part. They're dark and moody, looking plenty ripe for hiding in. And look, if you hand me a megastructure to explore, I'm going to do so. I'm also a fan of your main weapon, a crossbow. Not enough games with crossbows if you ask me! There's all sorts of bolts you can use with it, like a fire bolt that, obviously, sets things or enemies alight, a rope bolt to help you quickly climb or swing out of danger, a decoy bolt that makes a lot of sound to distract with, or a moss bolt; I'm not sure what that one does, my guess would be to dampen your footsteps and make it easier to sneak up on unsuspecting baddies.

Said baddies also appear to be infected with some kind of parasite, the severing of which appears to come in handy when trying to take them down. Overall, The Citadel Project likes a neat little im sim with just enough going on to make me curious to explore further. Which I might do, when I get the chance, as there is a demo available on Steam. Alternatively, I could just wait a week, as the game is out in early access November 11th, just over a week away. You can wishlist it on Steam right here.

#4043. "Steam's review queue is clogged up by AI slop": Salacious Fire Emblem-ish Food Devils gets a delay because its devs think Valve is inundated with genAI games

You might have seen that for today's grub, Edwin decided to in part feed The Maw with Food Devils, an incredibly salacious, foodie take on Fire Emblem, as it was meant to release today. The only problem is, it's not actually out yet. That might prompt you to call Edwin a rotten liar and march up to his castle at the top of the hill on a dark and stormy night with pitchforks and torches, but I beseech you to wait, because it's actually Steam's fault. And potentially, it's the fault of all those awful AI games that have been flooding Steam recently.

In a Steam blog post shared earlier today, developer Studio Daimon explained why the game isn't able to be released today, first offering a bit of context: if you want to put your game on Steam, you have to submit for approval so that it matches what you've described and doesn't harbour malware, amongst other reasons. As the post explains, "before submitting a build, devs see a disclaimer that says 'This review typically takes 3-5 business days, but please allow up to 7 business days in case feedback needs to be addressed'." Except the team submitted their build on October 12th, more than 20 days ago, with no approval in sight.

The reason? "We can only assume it's because Steam's review queue is clogged up by AI slop, but the whole process is now taking several weeks for some developers." For some context, Game Discovery Tool did some statistics magic and found that more than 50% of games released in October on Steam featured an AI disclosure. Valve have required that games disclose AI use since January 2024, and a year on from then in January 2025 only just over 14% of games featured such a disclosure. In January 2026, that jumped up to a little over 25%, and now here we are at more than 50%.

And to be clear, Steam releases have gone up too. According to SteamDB data, a little over 2000 games were released on the platform in October 2025. But in October 2026, that has jumped up to almost 4000. Correlation is obviously not causation, so take that with a pinch of salt. Still, it paints a concerning image over AI usage, and potentially sounds like it's affecting how Valve operates. Almost as if allowing free reign over AI is bad, or something!

Unfortunately for Studio Daimon, there's no estimate on when Food Devils might launch. "Even now, we don't know when Steam will give us the final OK to finally release our game," they wrote. "We sent another ticket last week saying that the situation was urgent and that we might miss our release date because of this, but it also got ignored. I'm sure that their staff is just too overwhelmed at the moment, but these sudden and massive delays have affected many developers throughout October, with some even being forced to postpone their releases... including us."

They're hoping to still be able to release it by the end of the week, but "can't make any plans or promises because it's out of our control." Perhaps in the meantime, for those who like what's cooking in the devs' kitchen, we could throw the game a wishlist to be ready for whenever it does launch.

#4042. Three New Console Features Begin Rolling Out Today For Xbox Insiders (November 12)

Including a "Shuffle" feature for dynamic backgrounds!

The announcements are coming thick and fast today! This latest one is for Xbox Insiders, and it concerns three new console features that are rolling out now to members of the Alpha Skip-Ahead tier (with more tiers followed by a public release in the future).

Arguably the most notable one is the ability to rotate dynamic backgrounds - this means can turn on the "Shuffle" feature to display different backgrounds on a hourly, daily or weekly basis. You can also now organise your Xbox Disc to Digital titles more effectively, while there's even the ability to move the Xbox guide over to the right!

Let's take a look at all three features, and you can let us know what you think of them in the comments.

On this page: Three New Console Features Begin Rolling Out Today For Xbox Insiders (November 12)

To save a favorite, go to Settings > General > Personalization > My background > Dynamic backgrounds > Dynamic backgrounds, choose a background, and press X. You’ll find it in the new Favorites category. Pro tip: If you have a controller with an exclusive background, like the XBOX Wireless Controller X25 Special Edition, saving that background as a favorite lets you use it even when the controller isn’t connected!

You can also choose Shuffle at the start of any background category. Have your background change each time you sign in, or set it to change hourly, daily, or weekly. Shuffle your favorites or explore a whole category, it’s an easy way to keep Home feeling fresh.

Starting today, XBOX Insiders who’ve claimed a digital license from a disc-based games will see those games in a separate category in their full library. Prefer to keep them alongside your other owned games? You can switch back in Settings > General > Personalization > Games & apps. From that same page, you can also hide the digital license icon on game tiles.

Prefer the guide on the right? Now you can put it there. XBOX Insiders can choose whether the Guide opens on the left or right side of the screen to switch up how you navigate XBOX. Pick your side in Settings > General > Personalization > Guide. Tell us if you’re team left or team right.

#4041. Mini Review: Sonic Pico Park (Switch) - Charming Puzzle-Platformer Returns With A Nostalgic Co-Op Collab

Pico Park is a fascinating success story for developer Shunsuke Miyake, who created the original game over a decade ago while working at Sega. A cute, minimalist and deceptively challenging puzzler, it exploded in popularity with the introduction of online co-op and a feature-packed sequel that was released on Switch in 2024.

This new spin-off takes the escalating challenge of multiple puzzle modes and invites Sonic and his ever-expanding menagerie of friends to the party. Available on both Switch 1 and 2, Sonic Pico Park takes the core mechanics of Pico Park and adds a suite of design features from the Blue Blur's 16-bit heyday.

Challenges range from effortless, like walking forward and pressing a button, to lateral conundrums involving spikes and insta-kill barriers. Other mechanics offer slightly taxing fun, especially anything that requires the party to be tethered together. Then there are the absolutely punishing experiences that will have you yelling at each other or laughing your heads off (sometimes both).

Three distinct modes offer a balanced spread of co-operative and adversarial challenges. World Mode separates 15 distinct puzzle scenarios into four stages of increasing difficulty. Battle pits teams against each other to collect the most rings. Endless has you run a gauntlet, trying to last the longest without making a mistake.

All of this is livened up by the inclusion of Sonic and pals, with some nicely presented nostalgia to help ring (pun intended) in his 35th anniversary. All of the series' characters are selectable, with a couple specifically tuned for large-character puzzles, like Big the Cat. The series' iconic rings form the basis of Battle mode while also adding an extra mechanic to certain puzzles that require precise calculation of invincibility frames. Elsewhere, there's a pinball minigame and a top-down version of the Sonic 2 bonus stage.

It's a great game to play on the go, although you will need others, because there is no solo play available. Its bright colours and visually sparse stages are complemented by simple controls well suited to the Joy-Con. There's also something deeply satisfying about hearing those classic Sega sound effects coming out of the undocked speakers.

Sonic Pico Park is a good little game for multiple players to have fun with, and it more than caters for Sonic fans looking for yet another nostalgia fix.

#4040. Ubisoft are reportedly tapped as one potential company that could acquire Arkane, though the Dishonored studio's own management may be in the running too

I'd really like it if it weren't Ubisoft though

Things are potentially looking up for Arkane, depending on how you feel about Ubisoft (and depending on who actually ends up acquiring them). I mention the Assassin's Creed developer because, reportedly, they're interested in buying the studio from Microsoft, having even made a bid for it. I'll go out on a limb here and say it's the whole being French thing, but uh, I'd really rather someone else bought Arkane.

This comes from, you guessed it, Bloomberg, who say that sources they've spoken with claim two other gaming companies have also made a bit. There is even the potential that Arkane would be sold to their own management, as Xbox are considering such a move. But overall, it doesn't yet sound like anything is leaning any particular way, as Xbox haven't formalised a deal with any of the potential buyers. Bloomberg also note that if a deal is made, this should then allow Arkane to finish their work on their Blade game, which is expected to release within the next couple of years.

Apparently an Xbox spokesperson told Bloomberg that the gaming company is exploring their options ahead of their December deadline, but didn't comment any further. Ubisoft reportedly did not have a comment to make on the matter. For some context on that December deadline, because of French labour laws, companies that have over 1000 staff members are required to search for a buyer for three months before they can just completely shut down. That makes December 13th the final date that such a deal has to be made by, meaning there's about a month and a half left to go.

Arkane's sale comes as part of a sweeping range of cuts, sales and closures being made by Microsoft at the moment. In July, it was announced that studios like Double Fine, Undead Labs and Compulsion would no longer be a part of Xbox, with all three going indie; Ninja Theory was also announced as part of these cuts, but unfortunately it's looking like they'll be shutting their doors. Thousands of Xbox staff were also laid off at this time, with more laid off in September, and even more coming this month and January reportedly. As always, solidarity with all workers affected by Microsoft's heartless and money hungry cuts.

#4039. God of War: Sons of Sparta Really Will Be Ported Backwards to PS4

Out on 16th Nov, with a free update for PS5 owners

It's now been confirmed God of War: Sons of Sparta, the mostly forgotten Metroidvania game that launched earlier this year, will indeed be ported back to PS4.

Having debuted on PS5 in February, the PS4 version launches next week, on 16th November 2026.

For both current PS5 owners and any new players on PS4, the base title will be supported by two extra modes: Hermes Mode and Erebus Mode.

Hermes Mode is a speedrun challenge featuring a split-based timer and a scoreboard. You automatically unlock the mode by finishing the game, or you can enter the following cheat code on the main menu to access it straight away:

Hermes Mode Code: Up Up Down Down Left Right Left Right L1 R1 Touch Pad

Then there's Erebus Mode, which revolves around both you and the enemy dying from one hit. It's dubbed the "ultimate challenge" for God of War: Sons of Sparta.

When it launched on PS5 following a shadow drop reveal, Sons of Sparta didn't exactly set the world alight. We enjoyed the adventure, awarding it a 7/10 score in our God of War: Sons of Sparta PS5 review.

"It's a mostly successful experiment; the Metroidvania structure works well with the franchise's mechanics, and it looks and sounds the part. However, it takes too long to really come into its own, leaving the early parts of the game feeling a bit lacking compared to the richer experience found later on."

We were one of the few who did, though, as the overall critic rating on Metacritic sits at a 64.

Now on a less powerful system, it's not like a PS4 version can fix any of its problems. At least it gives those people still using a PS4 a chance to play the game.

Wolfenstein 3 is officially in the works at MachineGames, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma has announced.

Sharma has been firing off semi-big announcements via her official Twitter account all day in celebration of Xbox's 25th anniversary, including confirmation that Id Software is working on a new game, but this is undoubtedly the biggest news of the bunch.

"Wolfenstein 3 is officially in production at @MachineGames," reads a tweet from Sharma. "One of gaming's most important franchises, and a team that has done remarkable work bringing it forward. Looking forward to sharing more."

Not much else was revealed about the Wolfenstein revival, but it's exciting to know it's a full-blown mainline entry and not a spinoff ala Young Blood (which I enjoyed, to be fair). This will be the first mainline entry in the legendary first-person shooter series since 2017's Wolfenstein 2: The New Colossus, which somehow was almost 10 years ago.

Wolfenstein 3 is officially in production at @MachineGames. One of gaming's most important franchises, and a team that has done remarkable work bringing it forward. Looking forward to sharing more. https://t.co/YyX8LrbTvhNovember 12, 2026

Remember when I said "not much else was revealed" about Wolfenstein 3? Well, that's because Sharma was generous enough to tease us with a picture appearing to show the first page of Wolfenstein 3's dialogue script, seemingly confirming the first chapter is called Nazitraz. The scene opens in the inside of an interrogation cell with a conversation between longtime Wolfenstein protagonist William Joseph "B.J." Blazkowicz and a German-speaking character called Otto, which could be a number of bad guys throughout Wolfenstein history. B.J.'s longtime right hand, Fergus, also seems to be in the scene, but that's about everything that can be inferred based on what's shown.

MachineGames has been Bethesda's trusted Wolfenstein developer since 2014, starting with Wolfenstein: The New Order.

No details regarding platforms or release timing were revealed.

#4037. "An outright ban will not eliminate AI from the modding process," Nexus Mods say as they rule out barring generated creations from their site

"We drew the line where the real argument is"

The owners of Nexus Mods have ruled out instituting an outright ban on AI-generated works being uploaded the site, instead opting to expand their current rules on modders disclosing how they've used AI in making their mods. This latest move to address the waves of AI-created or AI-thumbnailed mods now hitting Nexus Mods on a daily basis follows Nexus' modus operandi up to this point, which has been simply to try and ensure AI usage is clearly labelled so prospective downloaders can make informed decisions.

"We won't introduce an outright ban on AI-generated mods," Nexus Mods owner and CEO Victor 'Foledinho' Folmann wrote in a news post. "You may ask me why, since that is not the solution some of you were looking for. The answer is simple: AI is currently used throughout the whole process of creation, from script autocompletion to generation of textures, voices, and full assets, and it is difficult to draw a clear boundary between what is acceptable and unacceptable. An outright ban will not eliminate AI from the modding process, but will prevent people from mentioning its use. We'd prefer the opposite; it should be out in the open, clearly labelled, and regulated according to the rules that we can implement on our platform.

"This doesn't mean that any work done using AI will get removed; AI-generated mods are welcome on our platform provided that they meet certain criteria regarding permissions, transparency, presentation, and conduct. Mod Authors should have a chance to decide about the further use of their work, and you should be able to decide for yourselves how much AI-based content you want to see, whether more, less, or no content at all.

"As for our own position: Nexus Mods will not use your mods to train AI and will not sell or license them to anyone doing so. We refused to do that in the past, and we will refuse to do so in the future. Given such a variety of opinions within our community, not everyone will agree with any decision taken. These are the ones we believe are right for Nexus Mods today, and we’ll keep adjusting them as the tools evolve and as we see how these changes work in practice, with your feedback guiding that."

In terms of the changes which are being brought in to toughen up the site's current three tag system design to make mods containing AI-generated content, AI media, or made with AI assistance easier to spot, Nexus are making AI disclosures mandatory for those uploading new mods. "What this means is that for mods tagged as AI-assisted, we’re also introducing a requirement for a public explanation of how and where AI was used, which should give you a better understanding of what you’re downloading, rather than leaving you to make assumptions on a tag alone," Folmann wrote. "We’re also going to make AI tags on mod pages more prominent, displaying them immediately after adult-content tags so they’re easier to spot."

"While we hope these changes will encourage everyone to disclose their AI usage, to be honest, that’s not going to happen," he continued. "Additionally, we are putting clear moderation standards in place, enforced with consequences for breaking the rules." New "permission options covering AI usage and training, as well as forks and derivative mods" are also being worked on, with the hopes of giving modders more control over how their works can be reused. Finally, Folmann noted that the site are "investing in security tooling and specialised staff" to address concerns over generative AI making "bespoke malicious code hidden inside mods" more prevalent.

Mod makers are being given a 60 day grace period to make sure their existing works meet the new rules, which'll run until January 2nd.

As you can imagine, the comments section of this Nexus Mods announcement is lively. Over on LinkedIn, Folmann patted himself on the back a bit about the mixed reception being an indicator the site are going about this the right way. "Some wanted a full ban. Some think we went too far. That tells me we drew the line where the real argument is," he declared, adding that "transparency beats prohibition". He also reiterated that his vision is of "modding that's Spotify-easy to play and GitHub-powerful to create, with humans in charge".

I reckon that with or without these changes, in the absence of its owners taking a strong stand browsing Nexus Mods is going to carry on be more of an exercise in ducking dodgy stuff than it was prior to most games' pages being splattered with the likes of icky AI-baked Geralt clones standing where decent screenshots of the actual game would've been more than adequate.

#4036. Nintendo's On The Hunt For A Digital Archivist To Preserve Its Rich History

With closing online storefronts, the move to digital media and the rise of streaming, there are few gaming industry topics more discussed right now than preservation. Fortunately, it looks like Nintendo is making an effort to ensure that its history doesn't get lost to time (thanks, Time Extension).

Nintendo of America is currently hiring a Digital Archivist to "support the preservation, organization, and accessibility of historical hardware and software information," according to the job description. In short, this person would be responsible for ensuring that all things Nintendo are kept safely stored away and easily accessible.

We're sure that there are a few of you lovely lot reading whose brains are already like a Nintendo archive, and it certainly sounds like the job comes with its fair share of perks. The chosen applicant will surely have unrivalled access to Nintendo's historical records, get the chance to "Interview subject matter experts and long-tenured employees to capture institutional knowledge," and organise one of the richest histories in gaming. Damn, and there we were getting a kick out of putting our important paperwork into colour-coded binders.

What's extra cool is that this will be the person responsible for finding and dishing out these records to anyone at Nintendo for future use — you know, for when someone comes asking who that moustachioed fella in the denim overalls is.

Of course, the job comes with a huge amount of technicalities, too. The listing requires "Experience developing metadata structures, taxonomies, classification systems, or naming conventions," is looking for someone familiar with "metadata and archival standards such as Dublin Core, DACS, EAD, PREMIS, MODS, or similar frameworks," and has at least two years of previous work in Records, Metadata, Knowledge, or Digital asset management. In short, it isn't for any old Joe.

But hey, what an opportunity! This is a 12-month contract based out of Redmond, WA, and it will presumably result in Nintendo's 100+ year history living on for many more to come.

If you think this one might be for you, you'll find even more about the job in the official listing.

Feature The Nintendo Museum Goes Hard On Merch & Fun, But Could Dive Deeper Into History

What do you make of this job listing? Let us know in the comments.

#4035. Xbox CEO Announces Major New Bethesda Games In The Works, Including Wolfenstein 3

"Wolfenstein 3 is officially in production at MachineGames"

Xbox boss Asha Sharma has been taking the opportunity today to announce multiple new Bethesda games that are in the works as Xbox first-party titles, including the long-awaited Wolfenstein 3.

Sharma made the announcement on social media while highlighting that Wolfenstein is "one of gaming's most important franchises", and the third entry is once again being helmed by Bethesda studio MachineGames.

Here's a look at her post with an accompanying teaser image:

Prior to this, the Xbox CEO also revealed that Bethesda studio id Software has begun work on its next game, while also hyping up a new "Slaughter Mode" update coming to DOOM: The Dark Ages Revelations next week.

The Verge editor Tom Warren reckons id Software's next title will be another entry in the DOOM series:

It sounds like both of these projects are still very much in their infancy as things stand, although it was rumoured back at the start of 2026 that performance capture was set to begin on the next Wolfenstein title.

We're just glad they've now been revealed - the two studios have a great track record delivering awesome games!

News Wolfenstein 3 'Casting Call' Reportedly Leaked, Performance Capture Set To Begin

It could still be years before we see it though

News DOOM Director Elaborates On The State Of The Studio Going Forward

"We're excited to share more of what we're working on"

Excited for Wolfenstein 3? How about a new DOOM? Let us know down in the comments section below.

Fraser is the News Editor at Pure Xbox, where he spends his time reporting on the biggest stories in the world of Xbox and beyond.

#4034. PSA: GTA 6 Does Not Have Online Multiplayer at Launch

GTA 6 is now less than a week away from its official launch, coming to PS5 on 19th November, 2026.

It's likely to become the biggest entertainment launch of all time, with excitement at a fever pitch coming off the back of GTA 5, which is the third best-selling game ever at a staggering 235 million copies.

Something that not everyone may know, however, is that GTA 6 will be a single-player game only at first; the online component will not be available initially.

This won't come as a shock to those in the know, as Rockstar Games has described it as a solo experience and has not yet referred to any form of online play.

However, it seems there are many expectant fans that are excited to hop straight into multiplayer with their buddies. In case you didn't know, you won't be able to do this when GTA 6 launches next week.

I suspect this confusion comes from just how long GTA 5 has been around. The game was first released on PS3 13 years ago, and GTA Online is almost as old, launching a couple of weeks after the main game.

Re-releases of GTA 5 on PS4 and PS5 have always arrived with GTA Online as part of the package, so even though the original game didn't have online multiplayer to begin with, it's been a constant presence for millions of players for well over a decade.

It makes sense that people have become accustomed to GTA 5 providing GTA Online, and took it for granted that its sequel would include the feature from day one. This is not the case.

For GTA 6, it's expected that an updated version of GTA Online will launch sometime in 2027, though an exact date has yet to be confirmed. It won't take a full year to appear, despite what this recent Bloomberg video inadvertently suggests.

It's believed that GTA Online will come to GTA 6 in a matter of a few months, possibly launching in the first quarter of 2027.

Rumour has it that the PC port of GTA 6 will launch in a similar timeframe, and it would make sense for these two things to be aligned.

So, to summarise: GTA 6 does not feature online multiplayer at launch, but it likely won't be too far off.

Avatar: Seven Havens season 2 has officially set its release date, and it's not too far away. The Legend of Korra sequel will release Book 2 on May 21, 2027.

Just like the first season, there will be 13 episodes in total, and they will air in three-episode chunks through to June 11. The next stage of Pavi and Nisha's journey is called 'Book Two: Discovery' and the synopsis teases plenty more adventure yet for the twins.

This reads: "Pavi continues her chakra journey to the Floating Isles and learns more about what happened to Korra. Meanwhile, Nisha discovers vital information about the mysterious spirit energy Pavi released from Ellora. The girls are brought together in New Ba Sing Se, along with all their unresolved issues."

Saheli Khan returns as Pavi in the new episodes, alongside Aishu Devan as Nisha, Akshay Khanna as Karthik, Major Curda as Jae, and Sakina Jaffrey as Agam. Paramount also doubled down on the future of the show, confirming that Book 3 and Book 4 are also planned, with the former also airing in 2027.

Speaking to GamesRadar+, executive producer Ethan Spaulding teased the show's new location in Book 2. "I'd say get your surfboards," he told us, suggesting a rewatch of the finale. "I think if you guys freeze-frame, you can kind of get a vibe of what that haven might be like. But yeah, it's a fun place."

Avatar: Seven Havens Book One is out now on Paramount Plus. For what else to watch, check out our guide to the best shows on Paramount Plus as well as our round-up of all the upcoming TV shows you need to know about.

#4032. Smash hit cyberpunk storekeeper Probably Stolen was originally a different, non-cyberpunk game that seemed destined to sink without trace

Publisher tinyBuild celebrates turnaround after very underwhelming demo numbers

Space station trading game Probably Stolen – Cyberpunk Shopkeeper Sim has been doing rather well on Steam, attracting over 162,000 concurrent players last night. I've been feeling the urge to fire it up again myself, after my brief launch-day trawl through its quagmire of black market economics and factional rivalries.

The game's big numbers come as a shock given that it began life as another, non-cyberpunk kiosk job sim called Deepspace Emporium, which still has a Steam page as of writing. Deepspace Emporium seemed doomed to fizzle out in obscurity. But publisher tinyBuild got behind it regardless, working with developers Questing Goose to overhaul the art direction and lay on extra brainchips. The gamble paid off.

"Probably Stolen was initially a game under a different name with a released demo," summarises tinyBuild CEO Alex Nichiporchik on Twitter. "That demo peaked at 28 concurrent players. We loved the concept and gameplay, and worked with the dev to reinvent the visuals and focus on what works design wise. This is the result."

The original Deepspace Emporium seems very similar to Probably Stolen in broad strokes. The core of the game is haggling with strung-out ne'er-do-wells, buying or selling goods of varying quality and legality in order to surf a fluctuating market and pay the rent. It's Papers, Please, but you're searching for fake watermarks on cigarette packets, and wondering whether you dare stock contraband weaponry. You also have to appease or outmanouevre factions with competing interests, from station security to underworld barons.

From what I've played, Probably Stolen essentially takes all that and pumps up the Netrunner parallels with posher visuals. Not having played the now-unavailable Deepspace demo, I can't say how much intrigue it adds to all the shady transactions going on beneath the hood.

I'm not blown away by Probably Stolen's pixelart – I find it quite flavourless, as depictions of cyberpunk space stations go – but it has pleasing texture. I am disproportionately fond of the rolled-up sleeping mat beneath my counter. Looks nicely padded! Still, the meat of this game is undoubtedly the vast collection of items you can get your greasy fingers on, with a choice of retail lines and vocational pathways such as gunsmith and chemist. You can sell rat corpses, tins of caviar, robotic hands, scavenged shotguns, and purple tubers of uncertain origin. I am Commander Silverhand, and this is my favourite store on the Citadel.

It's lovely to think of a developer transforming a probable write-off into a chart-topper by means of some canny plumping and reorganising. The situation is almost certainly more complicated than Nichiporchik makes it sound. Still, let's take the opportunity to reminisce moist-eyed about a few other games that underwent a dramatic visual transformation during development.

The obvious one is Team Fortress 2, which once upon a time looked like a prototype Silent Hill environment with some khaki toy soldiers. Gearbox worked similar sorcery upon Borderlands, which once looked like a hungover Fallout 3. The prevailing wisdom is that piping in some colour and whimsy propelled these games to greatness, but who knows, perhaps if they'd clung to the old "football stadium toilet bowl" vibe, they'd have made an extra billion apiece. Any other precedents come to your mind?

#4029. "Keep talking about it": Raw Power Games call for Wishlist aid as they, and their historical strategy sandbox Chronicles: Medieval, lose funding

Raw Power Games, an independent studio comprising veteran developers of The Witcher 3, Total War: Three Kingdoms, and Crusader Kings III (among others), have called on players for support after losing their funding - an existential threat to both the organisation and to their debut, the still-in-development historical strategy game Chronicles: Medieval.

In a statement posted last week, Raw Power announced that "the necessary funding" behind the studio was no longer in place, despite Chronicles: Medieval – which was unveiled last year with an expensive-looking, Tom Hardy-narrated trailer – apparently being within touching distance of its planned early access launch. Hardy or no Hardy, however, the statement declared that they aren't "going down without a fight", hinting at talks with what could be possible new investors, asking interested would-be fans to "keep talking about" the game, and encouraging its inclusion on Steam Wishlists.

A few days on, the impact of this rallying call remains unclear. Raw Power Games have made no further statements, and Chronicles: Medieval does not seem to appear on Steam's own list of Top Wishlisted games. SteamDB have it at #26 in their desire-o-rankings, representing no change from its position immediately before the funding announcement was made, and while the game's Steam follower count has increased by over 1,000 week-on-week – significantly more so than surrounding games in the list – that doesn't feel like the kind of wild grassroots support that might save a dozens-strong studio.

Still, as my childhood television used to say, every little helps, and I'm inclined to hope for Raw Power's survival if only as an antidote to the enthusiasm-poisining dread of seeing so many other developers being laid off and shut down. Chronicles: Medieval looks promisingly ambitious too, mashing up sprawling Mount & Blade-style battles with an RPG-flavoured strategy layer that involves the player's custom-created character ascending the snooty social hierarchy of 14th century England. Best of luck to everyone trying to get it over the early access line.

#4027. Metaphor: ReFantazio Switch 2 Patch To Resolve Colour Glitch

Metaphor: ReFantazio arrived on the Switch 2 this week, and while the port has been well-received by fans and critics alike, there's one issue you may encounter.

Sega (and Atlus) have acknowledged this an official Japanese post about the game's release. Fortunately, it's not a game-breaking bug or anything like that, it just changes the colours of objects and characters. Here's a rough translation:

Atlus: "We have confirmed that after playing for a certain period, some objects and characters temporarily display colors different from their original colors. This bug does not affect game progress.

"We are preparing an update patch to fix this bug. When the stream begins, we will announce it on the official X account and official website."

As noted, a patch to address this issue is already in the works. This bug apparently can appear after 30 hours of gameplay.

Alongside this news, Atlus has also shared a special illustration to commemorate the release of this title on the Switch 2 this week. The artwork is from the game's character designer Shigenori Soejima.

If you aren't already playing this game on the Switch 2, there's a demo you can download from the eShop (save data also carries over), and you can find out more information about this version of the title in our review here on Nintendo Life.

#4026. Marvel has now given Doctor Doom the same number of appearances as Thanos in just over a year

VisionQuest's post-credits scene ups his appearance count

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Despite being a late addition swap-in as Marvel's big new villain, Doctor Doom has now had the same number of appearances as Thanos. Before 2018's Avengers: Infinity War, Thanos appeared in two end-credit scenes for The Avengers (2012) and Avengers: Age of Ultron (2015), as well as in the story of Guardians of the Galaxy (2015), all setting him up as the MCU's big bad.

Marvel hasn't had the same luxury of time with Doom, as one Twitter user pointed out, after he was announced in 2024 following Jonathan Majors being axed as Kang. As a result, the studio has been speedrunning his introduction, including him in three post-credits scenes in just over a year.

His first silent appearance came at the end of Fantastic Four: The First Steps in July 2025, when he's seen speaking to a young Franklin Richards before Sue Storm walks in. His second two appearances saw him recruiting new team members for his nefarious plans.

In Avengers: Endgame Encore, he finds Bruce Banner being held in a prison post-Spider-Man: Brand New Day before taking him away. His most shocking appearance then came at the end of VisionQuest, when he resurrects Scarlet Witch, telling her that her power will be his.

Doctor Doom now has the same number of appearances as Thanos had before Infinity War https://t.co/Wm1EibapW0November 11, 2026

It's been a pretty quick turnaround of set-up for Doom ahead of Doomsday, but it does mean we have some insight into what he's planning ahead of the movie's December release. It seems he's been recruiting several powerful figures to help in his fight against the Avengers.

Marvel fans have been reacting to the appearances, and it's fair to say that opinions are pretty mixed. "Thanos sent the army & Loki on Earth in 2012, & was the presence looming over the entire Guardians of The Galaxy AND there were a ton of people that were connected to him & suffered a lot because of him, seeking him," one wrote on Twitter, adding: "Btw I'm not saying this to trash Marvel with Doom, I can't wait for Doomsday, but yes, I wish they had him felt more to build up the DEPTH of the hype."

Meanwhile another wrote: "Honestly, they handled the switch from Kang to Doom really well, given the obvious reasons for it." A third then tweeted: "Imagine if Doom was planned from the start: his face with the hammer sound in Endgame (2019), Wanda in Doctor Strange (2022), Loki visiting Steve and the TVA’s fear in Loki's series, Bruce's kidnapping in Spider-Man BND, All set up years ago instead of added later."

Avengers: Doomsday hits UK cinemas on December 16 and US theaters on December 18. For more upcoming superhero movies, here's our guide to new Marvel movies and shows on the way.

Most of these are free to claim through in-game stores or redemption codes, but it's worth saying the Modern Warfare 4 M4 skin - arguably the best anniversary cosmetic of the lot - will require some sort of spending.

Available automatically to all Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024 owners, these commemorative liveries are available in the Aircraft Livery menu for the Boeing 737 MAX, XCub, Hot Air Balloon, and Skyship 600.

Designed as a tribute to 25 years of XBOX, the Inner Circuit Blueprint takes cues from classic translucent Xbox hardware. Its transparent green finish exposes the weapon’s internal systems, turning the technology beneath the surface into part of the visual identity.

#4024. Fate of the Galaxy is a huge, fully-featured Star Wars space combat sim that, thanks to being a total conversion mod for Freespace Open, even runs on my rubbish laptop

Star Wars has been back in the news recently because, to cut a long story short, the US alt-right have decided that Darth Vader was actually the good guy. We are not here to indulge such buffoonery. We are here to talk about Fate of the Galaxy, a free unofficial space combat simulator set during the events of the original Star Wars trilogy, featuring several mission-based campaigns and a stable of Imperial and Rebel Alliance ships that ranges from the quad-blasting X-Wing to Boba Fett's Firespray 31. Also, Naboo starfighters, if you really must.

It's a total conversion of poor dead Volition's venerable dogfighter FreeSpace 2, running on the open source Free Space 2 Open engine via the popular Knossos launcher. You don't need a copy of FreeSpace 2 to play it. You also don't need to pay. And nor do you need a whizbang PC – this bucket of bolts hums along happily on my i5-1145G7 with no dedicated graphics card. As the Rancor said to the padawan: finally, some good food.

Fate of the Galaxy has been in development off and on for almost two decades, weathering a number of team changes and shifts of focus. The FreeSpace Wiki has a longer account of its travels. It's not an officially licensed Star Wars production, as made evident by a scrolling text intro which takes the official orchestral theme and moves every note up or down a place, as though spitefully jolting the piano around under John Williams' fingers. It's not quite as bizarre as Portsmouth Sinfonia's Also sprach Zarathustra but it did make me cackle like the Emperor contemplating a freshly made asteroid field. But then I began playing, and my presumptuous merriment became a frown of concentration.

While hardly Steel Battalion, Fate of the Galaxy is a proper nerdy sim with a bustling 3D cockpit and all sorts of keyboard shortcuts to try once and immediately forget. You'll need to funnel energy between fore and aft shields during bombing runs on Star Destroyers, target individual subsystems with your ion cannon, give orders to other pilots, and consider whether to synch different guns for maximum effect. I can run the game fine on my work laptop with integrated graphics, but I'm definitely feeling the need for a beefier keyboard. And also a joystick. Certainly, I'm not going to get far in LAN multiplayer with this hunk of junk.

It seems a very generous production, based on 30 minutes playing kiss-chase with TIE bombers. The story campaigns and quickfix stand-alone skirmishes aside, there's a mission editor with text-based files for easier sharing. There's also VR support with head-tracking, should you own one of those haunted helmets. Learn more via the online manual (Google Doc), and find Fate of the Galaxy itself on Moddb. You'll need around seven gigs of disc space.

This being the year 2026, there's the question of generative AI usage - a topic of much concern lately in modding circles. Fate of the Galaxy's official site boasts that all the visual assets were "made by humans only". I'm less sure about other aspects – there's seemingly some artificial VO during the tutorial, though it sounds like antiquated, less insidious robocaller software. The FreeSpace Open engine itself greatly pre-dates today's chatbot invasion. The original FreeSpace 2 launched in 1999 - a more civilised age, when everybody still thought Darth Vader was an arsehole.

#4023. Rimworld-inspired colony sim Stardeus gets a huge update representing a year's worth of expansion and revision, with new tools for evil AI overlords

"Stardeus is in an early stage in terms of bulk and complexity, but it's already a pleasant blend of interesting ideas that generate a mostly relaxing vibe," wrote gallant star captain.exe Sin Vega in our 2022 analysis of Rimworld-influenced colony manager Stardeus. "One to watch for sure." Well, let it not be said that we weren't watching.

Stardeus has received a gargantuan early access update that has been "a year in the making," according to developer Kodo Linija. It's still a game about being an AI running a badly damaged interstellar colony ship in top-down view – sending drones to restore the damage, before waking the quarrelsome human popsicles from their slumber. But the new version introduces a quest system and a new opening tutorial chain, the ability to form alliances with other starfaring factions, the possibility of lifelong injury due to failed surgery, and the timely option to become an evil AI and mind-control your crew with beta waves, amongst other dastardly antics.

It introduces a new interface and a new ship aesthetic, a trust system that governs the odds of a mutiny, and a revised colonist skill system. There's also a freshened-up ground combat element that's now built around "cover, suppression, stuns and fleeing", and a new approach to space battles that's all about managing Flux generated when you fire weapons or take shield damage. The update notes on Steam tote more than 1,500 changes, with the dev enthusing that there is "hardly a system in the game that wasn't rebuilt, reworked or expanded".

I confess, I hadn't heard of Stardeus before. It sounds like fun, in the Dwarf Fortressian sense. The 1.0 rollout is due in "approximately Q1 2027".

#4022. 'We Want to Create Franchises That Withstand Decades': Sony Reveals Ambition to Dominate Anime

Sony’s gradual transition from consumer electronics to entertainment giant is paying dividends, as the firm’s value continues to rise on the back of hits like Spider-Man: Brand New Day and the overall PlayStation business.

But the manufacturer has one big ambition that will bring all its divisions together: anime.

A big Bloomberg report, focusing on subsidiary Aniplex’s boss Atsuhiro Iwakami, shed some light on the firm’s strategy. It’s moving aggressively to dominate an industry that’s booming in popularity worldwide.

Iwakami points to Demon’s Slayer as justification for its approach.

Its first movie, 2020’s Mugen Soul, dethroned Spirited Away to become Japan’s highest-grossing film. Its successor, 2025’s Infinity Castle, went on to gross almost $1 billion worldwide.

Iwakami’s goal is simple: to find or create the next One Piece, a franchise that could become the centrepiece of its entertainment division for potentially decades to come.

As the article points out, anime unifies all of Sony’s divisions in an unprecedented way: content can be created by Aniplex, distributed by Crunchyroll and Sony Pictures, promoted by PlayStation (where there’s an inherent overlap in audiences), and even supported by Sony Music (anime theme songs et al are wildly popular).

To support its ambitions, the company has become one of the biggest investors in light novel powerhouse Kadokawa, and Iwakami admits it would invest in sector stalwart Shueisha as well should the opportunity arise.

But original content will be foundational to Sony moving forwards, as it faces aggressive competition from Netflix and Disney, both of which are competing for content in the wake of the anime boom.

Sony ultimately wants a franchise it owns outright, where it can control all merchandise sales and more.

It recently founded a new studio, Hayate, as part of a joint collaboration between Aniplex and Crunchyroll. Its remit is to create original anime for a global audience.

Next year, Sony will add an anime tab to the PS5’s homepage, giving it another opportunity to promote its content to players around the world.

I’m particularly interested to see if PS Studios is eventually recruited to create original games based on some of these properties, and how it approaches those.

Obviously, if the goal is to create franchises that reach as many people worldwide as possible, then exclusivity may not necessarily be the play here.

But while Sony already has a strong foot in the door, it admits it’s still at the start of its strategy right now. It’s going to be interesting to see how things evolve over the coming years.

#4021. Fable's Latest Showing Didn't Exactly Blow Our Socks Off

It's the first time the Xbox RPG didn't wow us

Here at Pure Xbox, we're rather stoked about Playground Games' revival of Fable. We were picking jaws up off the floor in June, then again at gamescom in August, and even left London FanFest feeling pretty jazzed with what we got to play of the upcoming RPG.

So, let it been known for the record, I fully expect Fable to be a brilliant RPG. Top class in execution, full of joy and wow moments aplenty, but what on earth was Xbox thinking promoting Fable with that four-minute gameplay video? C'mon gang!

The footage was revealed during Seattle FanFest as part of Xbox's 25th anniversary jollies, although most of it was stuff we'd sorta seen before, and the choice of location was questionable at best. See for yourself in the video above.

"Both myself and Craig had a chance to play this demo last weekend, and we both came away pretty darn impressed with what we'd played. That said, we also remarked to each other that we wished we'd had a chance to explore Albion and interact with NPCs, which is something we'll have to wait a little bit longer for."

Feature We've Finally Played Xbox's New Fable Reboot, And Here's What We Think So Far

We went hands on at the recent Xbox FanFest

Where we'd previously been gobsmacked by vibrant castle towns and lush wilderness, this latest setting felt rather basic and lacking in character or detail. It was just some generic cliffside. It's not necessarily bad, but it's hardly the sort of environment I'd think to stuff into a trailer meant to turn people onto Fable.

As the video goes on, we get a little combat featuring swords, archery, and a sprinkling of magic. It all looks good, and having played the combat myself, it feels fun. But it doesn't last long, nor does it show us anything new or particularly interesting. The quest itself is cut short and lacking, as though it's just been ripped from a spoiler-free section of the game.

Just to reiterate, I reckon Fable will come good. Every gameplay reveal up until this point has been great. Big fan. This one just feels a little odd, almost as if it was cobbled together last minute. That's not ideal when you're trying to convince players to pick up Fable when it launches on Xbox Series X|S, PC, and PS5 on February 23, 2027.

It's got Game of the Year written all over it

#4020. The Game Awards 2026 Nominees To Be Announced Next Week, Zelda And GTA 6 Eligible

Geoff Keighley's annual show is almost here!

We're now at the tail end of the year, and you know what that means, right? It's time to get ready for The Game Awards.

The annual show, hosted by creator Geoff Keighley, is taking place on 10th December 2026, and will announce the nominees for each award "live" next week on 17th November 2026.

Although the highly-anticipated release Grand Theft Auto 6 isn't out until 19th November 2026, it will be eligible for nomination. This means the Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake for Switch 2, which currently has a critic score of 96/100 on Metacritic, can also be nominated.

Here's the rundown about eligibility for nomination via The Game Awards FAQ and rules pages:

Games must be made commercially available to customers on or before Friday, November 20, 2026, at 9 p.m. PT. In the Players’ Voice category, games must ship on or before November 30, 2026.

While GTA 6 and Zelda are sure to steal at least some of the spotlight, there have been plenty of other amazing games released this year. Capcom's knocked it out of the park with Resident Evil Requiem and games like Pragmata & Onimusha: Way of the Sword. And Pokémon also surprised us with the relaxing life sim Pokopia.

Once again, The Game Awards will stream live on 10th December 2026 from the Peacock Theatre in Los Angeles. As usual, you'll be able to tune in on YouTube and various other streaming platforms. For the first time, the show will also be streamed in the video game Roblox.

#4019. Oblivion and Skyrim’s gap was bridged by forward-looking books about a murderous floating island, so why is The Elder Scrolls 6 stuck reanimating a world that’s stood still since 2011

Why the Umbri-hell has time stopped in Tamriel?

Long waits between mainline entries in a series aren’t a new phenomenon, if perhaps a bit more common nowadays due to big games' ballooning development cycles. It took about 23 years for BioWare’s Baldur's Gate 2 to be followed up by Larian’s Baldur’s Gate 3, though there were a decent amount of spin-offs and remasters peppered between the two.

The wait for The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel hasn’t stretched on that long quite yet, but as Bethesda finally revealed concrete details about it just in time for Skyrim's 15th birthday, it really hit home for me that TES VI will be tasked with restoring motion to a world where calendars have been stuck in the 201st year of the 4th era since 2011. Perhaps it’s because I’m still in my twenties and haven’t lived long enough to see that many things I like pause their forward march for this long before returning. There’s also a good chance my expectations of timelines rolling forward on a regular basis without the need for a whole new entry are coloured by the constant stream of new stuff fed into most games via updates and live service passes these days.

However, when I look back at the interregnum between the last two Elder Scrolls games, Oblivion and Skyrim, I can’t help but feel that what Bethesda and ZeniMax have packed into the gap between Skyrim and Sentinel might have done the latter no favours. Sure, The Elder Scrolls Online has arguably meant that there’s been far more for series fans to sink their teeth into between mainline games than ever before, but because the MMO's a prequel, none of its tales and lore push the Elder Scrolls' timeline forwards. Meanwhile mobile and card game spin-offs like The Elder Scrolls: Blades, The Elder Scrolls: Legends, and The Elder Scrolls: Castles have all either slotted in before Skyrim or not been tied to a specific point in time.

On one hand, that leaves the devs a nice clean slate to take the sixth entry wherever they like narratively upon the conclusion of the Dragonborn’s adventures. On the other, Bethesda has missed the opportunity to paint out the world and further set up the stakes for Sentinel in the interim. Back when we were waiting for Skyrim's original release, the developers were pumping out spin-off books that daubed some fresh adventures onto the Elder Scrolls' canvas.

I bought these books - 2009’s The Infernal City and 2011’s Lord of Souls - ages ago upon hearing their tales referenced in the sorts of Elder Scrolls lore videos which appeal to sad nerds of my ilk, but have only gotten around to reading past the opening chapters in recent months.

In hindsight, I think I bounced off them that first time because it just felt a bit weird to be reading about set characters getting up to adventures in Tamriel rather than setting off on them in the boots of my own custom created protagonist. I didn’t run into the same with The Witcher, as you’re seeing that world through Gerry from the River’s eyes no matter where you turn. Anyway, the two Elder Scrolls novels by American author Greg Keyes tell the tale of the Umbriel crisis which took place 48 years after the Oblivion crisis and about 153 years before Skyrim’s dragon crisis (Tamriel does love a crisis). The Umbriel crisis saw a floating island powered by souls and formed via some Daedric drama, carve a path of destruction from Black Marsh to the Imperial City. Yep, the empire’s not-Roman soldiers had to fight a flying hunk of land. At one point some mages had to float a legion up in the sky so they could get their bottoms kicked by Umbriel’s defenders.

As you might’ve gathered, the books take the opportunity to tell a story which - especially in terms of where tech was in 2009 - wouldn’t necessarily fit an Elder Scrolls game. Or, at least, not one of the more straight-laced variety Bethesda have made in their post-Morrowind days. A lot of time’s spent looking through the eyes of two characters who’ve snuck aboard Umbriel, the floating island, after it destroyed their hometown and have to adjust to the strange customs of its inhabitant lords and their underlings before finding ways to help take it down. On the ground, things take a more familiar form, as a very serious Dark Elf named Sul and a nepo baby Imperial prince trek across bits of Cyrodiil, Morrowind, and Elsweyr on a quest to do their bit in vanquishing the threat. Then, there’s a Penitus Oculatus spy named Colin trying to figure out if the Umbriel Crisis is an inside job of some sort and a few tales of regular Imperial troops working to evacuate citizens living in the floating island’s path. In an Elder Scrolls game, you’d get some of that, but not be able to hop from person to person chapter by chapter in the fashion the books do.

Umbriel slowly floats across Black Marsh, southern Morrowind and Cyrodiil with an army of zombies in tow, much like this article’s about to float into mildly spoilery territory for the two books. You see, The Infernal City and Lord of Souls outline what happened to cause the red year, a volcanic eruption which took the land of the Dark Elves from the beautifully alien place it was at the time of The Elder Scrolls 3 and reduced it to the ash-covered wasteland it’s outlined to be at the time of Skyrim. As the latter game’s lore books would subsequently set in stone, Baar Dau - the meteor suspended in the air above Vivec City at the time of Morrowind - fell and destroyed the city following the disappearance of the metropolis’ namesake ex-Tribunal god-king. The books reveal that the big rock didn’t fall the moment Vivec vanished, but was kept afloat by a device called the Ingenium, which is essentially a magic box powered by regular soul sacrifices. Two Dunmer, Vuhon and the aforementioned Sul, ended up having a fight rooted in the tech’s murderous nature and that’s actually what led Baar Dau to finally hit the ground.

Either way, the meteor falls, but that's not an insubstantial bit of backstory for a source outside of the games to add to the Elder Scrolls’ canon. Also wound into the tale of how Umbriel came to be is a bunch of extra flesh on the bone of the relationship between Daedric prince Clavicus Vile and Umbra. In the games, the latter’s always just been a powerful sword which imprints a new personality onto its wielder, but in the books it’s portrayed as a being capable of nicking some of Vile’s godly power and plotting to escape the prince’s realm of Oblivion via the building of Umbriel. Beyond those, the books also offer a chance to get to know emperor Titus Mede I, the warlord who took over the Empire following a post-Oblivion crisis interregnum and whose offspring you murder during Skyrim’s Dark Brotherhood questline.

None of this is anything close to required knowledge for playing Skyrim. No characters from the books pop up to say hello, likely because enough time’s passed for most to perish of natural causes. The sole reference I can recall comes via a chat about a location called Sleeping Tree Camp, which isn’t tied to any of the main questlines. You can, and I did for a long time, totally ignore these time-bridging tomes. That said, I do feel that having now taken the time to read them has helped me see the history of Tamriel as something not as strictly limited to the specific snapshots in time presented by each of the games.

Tales like these, which aren’t conveyed with as much natural emotional detachment as I tend to feel when reading much-condensed accounts of historical events or far off places on the pages of in-game lore books, really help in creating the illusion that The Elder Scrolls’ world is growing and evolving as our own does. It’s not just a snow globe that only shifts whenever some prophesied hero piloted by a controller or keyboard rocks up to shake it.

I do think, in large part due to the size of the real world gap between it and Skyrim, The Elder Scrolls 6 would have and still could benefit from having spin-offs like these to keep gently nudging the timeline forwards. A complicating factor is that judging by this week’s teaser, Sentinel seems like it could be set in the 206th year of the fourth era, a mere five years after the events of Skyrim. That’d mean no 200-ish years of wiggle room in which to slot some spin-off stories without serious risk of influencing things that’d have to be reflected in the new game. Unless Bethesda wanted to either put serious barriers up around where the spin-off could tread or get into a game of arbitrarily deciding what is or isn’t canon. With some collaboration, it could certainly be done, but it could also be a headache the studio wouldn’t want.

It’s likely too late to start the ball rolling now anyway, but that doesn’t stop it being worth asking why Bethesda and their famously adaptation-loving corporate bosses at Microsoft didn’t make sure they had something akin to these books in the works when Sentinel was punted down the road in favour of Starfield.

You did this well once, why haven’t you managed to pull it off again this time? I’m hoping that isn’t the inquiry which’ll come to define The Elder Scrolls 6 as much as questions about where a chunk of the old Bethesda magic had gone did with the studio’s trip to space. Lest the next long wait for a game from them be packed with even more uncomfortable silence.

Paul Bettany says they considered bringing Wanda back

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

VisionQuest came to a close with an epic season finale that saw Vision reunite with both of his sons, Billy and Tommy Maximoff. However, there was a missing member of the family: Wanda Maximoff. She's mentioned several times in the final few episodes but doesn't appear in the main series.

However, it turns out that they did consider bringing her back. Speaking to The Playlist, Vision star Paul Bettany said: "I remember having this conversation with [Kevin Feige], and he said, 'You and Terry [Matalas, showrunner] have done such a great job at making me care about Vision. I really don't think you should distract from that by giving the audience that at the end of the [show]. It will just fundamentally all become about WandaVision again, and this should and can stand on its own.' And I think he was right."

Of course, this doesn't mean that Wanda doesn't appear at all in the Disney Plus show. In the finale's second post-credits scene, Doctor Doom takes a trip to Mount Wundagore. We see Wanda pull down the mountain on top of her, as happened in Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness, before Doom appears and lifts the stones off of her. He brings her back to life before saying, "Scarlet Witch awaken, your power will be mine."

Elizabeth Olsen looks set to appear in Avengers: Doomsday then and a recent leak from Anthony Mackie seemed to confirm that Vision is coming back too. We may finally get a Maximoff reunion after all then, although probably not under the best of circumstances.

#4017. 'That's An Error' - Xbox Engineer Denies 360 Games Are Being Teased For Disc To Digital

Update [Fri 13th Nov 2026, 5:45pm]: Well, unfortunately we have answer - Xbox engineer Eden Marie has confirmed over on BlueSky that the inclusion of Fable III in this image was an "error".

While the post itself is private, it reads as follows (and thanks to Pure Xbox user TheBillConiglio for alerting us to this):

"Bill: Seeing an image of a library with Fable 3 having a disc to digital badge. Error, or......"

Original Story: Yesterday, Xbox starting rolling out three new console features for Xbox Insiders to try out: rotating home backgrounds, the ability to choose which side the Xbox guide pops open on, and new ways to organise disc to digital games.

They're all cool features that we're definitely keen to play around with, but what got our attention most was the image Xbox used to show off the new disc to digital update. Particularly, the games featured with the D2D licence icon plopped in the bottom-left corner of each game tile.

Did Xbox just tease the inclusion of Xbox 360 games in the D2D programme? Well, that would be true if the image depicting Fable III is to be taken at face value. At a glance, you'd probably see the image above and think, 'great, that's awesome', but the more you look at it, the weirder it gets.

Avowed famously launched on Xbox without a physical disc. So, if the theory about Xbox 360 games joining the programme is on the money, does that mean we're getting a physical copy of Avowed too? And what about Age of Empires IV? That never received a physical release either. Then If we really want to go Enola Holmes on this image, Forza games aren't D2D compatible.

We're thinking someone at Xbox might've messed up with this image. Announcements of this magnitude shouldn't be buried in an Xbox Insider update. Xbox should be shouting about it on the front page. So, why do an Xbox 360 game and two digital-only titles have D2D icons attached to them? I could think of a lazy reason.

Only time will tell, but consider us sceptical for now. We've chalked this one up to a blunder from Xbox, although it wouldn't surprise us if Xbox 360 games did eventually join the D2D programme. And hey, it's Xbox's birthday this Sunday. Maybe there's more to this than meets the eye.

@BacklogBrad the issue isn't with converting 360 or OG XBox game discs to digital versions, the issue is that those discs don't have a unique identifier assigned to them (this started with the XBox One generation, and not all of the early XBox One games have them).

Without the UID there's no way to assign a specific disc to the digital license, meaning one disc could be used to grant anyone digital access to that game. The UID prevents this as you need to revalidate the disc licence periodically, and if you sell the disc / lend it to someone, it will validate on their device, which will invalidate your license the next time your console does an online check in.

I hope they find a way to make it happen as it'd be awesome to add our XBox & 360 games to our digital libraries. Plus with this breakthrough it'd give Sony no reason not to follow suit and implementing a D2D feature of their own (i.e. Copy XBox's solution to the problem).
